It suits surfers who are fast to their feet and comfortable with coral flying close under-fin.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Half Moon Bay is the main beach on Antigua's East Coast, set inside a National Park that doubles as a relaxed family day out with good snorkelling reefs close by. The reef off the northern headland shapes the surf here, feeding a sucky take-off that runs into fast, punchy walls with a bit of speed and power. Waves peel both left and right, and swell can wrap into the bay and clean up a little.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Hawksbill Bay is a series of four crescent beaches breaking over uneven reef, and while the beaches themselves are highly regarded, the surf is pretty disorganized. Several reefs between Landing Bay and Hawksbill hold decent waves, though some sit in front of the hotels and are private. Offshore, Sandy Island can turn on for all-time conditions, but it takes the fickle combination of good north swell and no wind, plus a boat to get there.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Palmetto Point is a righthand sandbar barrel on the west coast of Barbuda, breaking over sand along a stunning pink-sand beach. When it fires, it throws serious tubes in very little water right up against the shore, and the take-off is tricky because the wave breaks close to the sand and never really lets up. The setting is pristine and remote, and the west and south coasts are usually flat unless a hurricane has moved into the area.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Spanish Point sits on the southeast tip of Barbuda, where a barrier reef throws sectioning lefts alongside a few scruffy rights that only break cleanly when the wind goes calm. A line of barrier reefs runs parallel to the eastern shore, but onshores usually shred them apart, so they come alive only on a rare westerly or windless day. Just nearby, Two Foot Bay has easy access and a gap in the reef that may hold some rights.

guideSummary.surfForecast: Arashi Beach in Aruba is an exposed beach break. The best conditions for surfing are during the hurricane season. Works best in offshore winds from the east northeast and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the northwest. The beach break provides left and right handers. It's sometimes crowded here. Beware of urchins and rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Freights probably has the best lefts on the south coast, but it needs a big south swell to really line up. When it is on, the wave is long, fast and hollow, breaking over dead coral in three defined sections: feathered walls off the cliffs at the point, barrels through the central reef, and, with a bit of luck, more bowls on the inside. Smaller days show a completely different side of the place, with plenty of shorter rights and lazy longboard shoulders that make it a genuinely useful beginner spot.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Sand Bank, also known as Cattlewash, is a shifty sand-bottom beachbreak just north of Soup Bowl, on the far side of the rocky outcrop past the Edgewater Inn. It's often sloppy and rarely lines up cleanly, but when the sand sets up right it can throw a dumping right-hand bowl or peel as an A-frame with both lefts and rights.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Sandbank on the East Coast is an exposed beach break that has consistent surf Works best in offshore winds from the southwest. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Soup Bowls is Barbados's famous east coast right, a powerful, intense reef wave breaking in front of Bathsheba. It serves up vertical drops, thick bowls, and big shut-down sections. There's a lot of water behind it, so the wave runs deep and grinding, and slowing down enough to find the barrel is sometimes the real challenge.

There are shorter, bowly rights on offer too, though they catch more of the wind than the lefts do.

It breaks over a dead coral platform that stays fairly benign and serves up soft, crumbly lefts that peel and trickle down into the bay. A few against-the-grain rights turn up too, and the whole set-up leans toward fun, easy rides.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Apple Bay, known to locals as Capoon's Bay, is a small nook of coast with a wide open window to the north and a reef that delivers both rights and lefts. In front of the famed Bomba Shack sits a perfectly A-shaped reef that grooms incoming swell into clean, ruler-edged walls. It's the most consistent surf spot in the BVI, and when the swell lines up it's a genuinely fun wave.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Brewers Bay is a tranquil, protected bay that spends most of its time flat, throwing up little more than dribblers. When a strong north pulse finally pushes into the bay, it comes alive with rapid, punchy pointbreak-style lefts peeling along the headland reef over live coral. There's also a rarer right further out in the bay that the pros love.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Brewers Bay in Tortola is an exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Works best in offshore winds from the south southeast. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell angle is from the northwest. The beach breaks consists of lefts. Relatively few surfers here, even on good days. Surfing here means negotiating dangerous rips.

Throaty barrels stand up at the tip of the point over shallow coral heads, race down the line into an inside bowl, then shoulder off into deep water around the corner.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Capoon's Bay, also known as Little Apple Bay, sits on the north shore of Tortola, the largest island in the British Virgin Islands. There's also a softer right on the east side of the main peak, often used by SUPers and known as Gay Rights.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Cappoons Bay is a small stretch of coast with a wide open window to the north, northwest and northeast, and the reef sitting in front of the famous Bomba Shack is the reason to come. It's a perfectly A-shaped reef that grooms incoming swell into ruler-edged walls, throwing both rights and lefts over coral and rock. It's the most consistent surf spot in these islands, and when the swell has a little west in it the left comes to life and the rights bowl up nicely.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Capoons Bay in Tortola is an exposed reef break that has pretty consitent surf. Winter and spring are the favoured times of year to visit. Offshore winds blow from the southeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the north. Reef breaks provide lefts and rights. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Beware of rocks,reef,urchins,jellyfish and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Josiah's Bay is a wide sand beach tucked into the north-facing coast of Tortola, with A-frame peaks scattered along its length. The waves are slopey and often on the weak side, which makes it a forgiving place to learn, and it sits slightly off the beaten track. When the sand, tide, and wind all line up, though, Josiah's can still throw the occasional beachbreak barrel.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Josiahs Bay in Tortola is a quite exposed beach break that has very consistent surf. Winter and spring are the best times of year to visit. Offshore winds are from the northeast. Groundswells and windswells are equally likely and the ideal swell direction is from the north. The beach break offers mainly right hand waves. Rarely crowded here. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here.

The peak sits a long paddle offshore, and on a windless day it splits into two very different waves: a long, relaxed left and a much more intense, hollow right.

guideSummary.surfnerd: West End is a long right-hand point tucked away on Anegada, a coral island unlike anywhere else in the British Virgin Islands. Its highest point sits just 10 m / 30 ft above sea level, so the whole place looks like one giant beach, and the surrounding reef is a well-known diving area. For most of the year West End Point is really a windsurf spot, with wide open exposure to the wind that also suits kiting and sailboarding.

Waves break over sand and lava, producing both beach and reef setups with rights and lefts.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Windmills is the best-known surf spot on Cuba's south coast, a ledgy and unpredictable right-hand reefbreak that breaks over dead coral. It's a rare catch, though: this coast only really turns on during hurricane swells or a bit of southeast windchop, so most of the time the surf is happening elsewhere. When Windmills isn't working, the wider region has options like the Cajobabo rivermouths, the Playa Juragua lefts, and the beachbreak peaks at Playa Aguadores and Playa Mar Verde on either side of Santiago de Cuba.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Encuentro is a corner of reef at the western end of Cabarete beach, out past Sosua and not far east of Puerto Plata, in the windsurfing and kitesurfing capital of the Caribbean. The coast here is wide open to the tradewinds and dotted with offshore reefs, and Encuentro itself serves up a long left alongside a short, bowly right, with swell and wind direction deciding which one is the pick of the day. The coral bottom and nice Caribbean water round out a genuinely good setup.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Encuentro in Amber Coast is an exposed reef break that has reliable surf. Winter and spring are the best times of year to visit. The best wind direction is from the south. guideSummary.surfnerd: Sosua is a left-hand reef pass on the Dominican Republic's north coast, and one of the few true reef pass waves in the region. It breaks over coral in nice Caribbean water, and the inside bowl is the part that really comes alive. The reef is shallow, so it deserves respect.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Sosua Bay in Amber Coast is an exposed reef break that has very consistent waves. Winter and spring are the favoured times of year to visit. The best wind direction is from the southeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the north. There is a right breaking reef. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Watch out for urchins and rocks.

Just up the coast, Anse Laborde is worth a look if you're exploring the area.

The beach breaks are all lefts. Sometimes crowded. Watch out for - Urchins.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Anse Couleuvre is a trade-wind protected right-hander tucked on the lee side of a big Caribbean island, framed by raw cliffs and a jungle backdrop. It's a narrow-window wave that only fires occasionally through the winter months. The ride opens with a manageable drop into a wall that wraps around the coral heads and turns very hollow in sections before racing through to the inside.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Anse Couleuvre on the North Coast is a fairly exposed reef break that does not work very often. Winter and spring are the best times of year to visit. Offshore winds are from the southeast with some shelter here from northeast winds. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the north. A reef breaks right. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of urchins, rips and rocks.

The beachbreaks along this stretch tend to close out quickly, which is why they mostly draw bodyboarders hunting for launch ramps.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Bagasse is a powerful reef break at the northern tip of the island near Grand-Rivière, one of two quality waves in the area. It throws barreling rights and lefts over a shallow, uneven reef shelf, with sucky, slabby sections built for surfers chasing tubes. The newer harbour has reshaped the set-up, and on the biggest wrapping swells or rare west swells a long right can peel down the harbour entrance.

A choice of left and right reefs. It's sometimes crowded here. Take care of urchins, rips and rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Pelle á Tarte is a shallow, powerful reef break that sits a short walk or a 15-minute paddle from the neighbouring setup. It runs much shallower and more punchy than its neighbour, throwing a hollow but makeable right alongside a death-defying left that only a handful of bodyboarders dare to take on.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Pelle a Tarte on the North Coast is an exposed reef break that has dependable surf. Winter and spring are the optimum times of year to visit. Offshore winds blow from the south southeast with some shelter here from northeast winds. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the north. The reef provides both left and right breaks. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Watch out for urchins, rips and rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Petit Havre is a quality left that starts in a zone of uneven reef and runs down to a small west-facing beach. It is the kind of wave that offers a bit of everything: short barrels on the reef section and long, slashable shoulders as the wall runs on. That mix pulls in plenty of surfers from the capital, and the setup also gives some shelter from northeast and east wind.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Petit Havre in Grande Terre is an exposed beach and reef break that has reasonably consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Works best in offshore winds from the northwest. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the southeast. The beach break provides left and right handers and a left hand reef break too.. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Often Crowded. Take care to avoid the rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Plage des Surfeurs sits in the Anse Bonneville, about 2 km from the fishing port of Tartane, and it's the best known and most consistent spot on the island, even if it often turns messy. This is a flexible bay with something for everyone, from lycra-clad learners to pig-dogging pros, which is why most contests run here or at Base-Pointe. After paddling around a large coral patch, you can surf mellow rights and lefts, with the longer rides coming off the rights.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Plage des Surfeurs on the North Coast is an exposed reef break that usually has waves. Winter and spring are the optimum times of year to visit. Offshore winds are from the south southeast with some shelter here from northeast winds. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the north. Primarily a right hand reef break, although a left is also possible.. Sometimes crowded. Watch out for urchins, rips and rocks.

The walls are soft, forgiving, and evenly paced, shouldering off for what can be a very long ride.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Ginsu is the main spot on Haiti's north coast, a fast, very ripable right over live coral. Haiti's original surfers, brothers Russell and Vadim Berhmann, named it after a famous brand of American cutlery, and Russell's line about it says plenty: "If the lip doesn't catch you, the razor reef will." He also reckons few spots in the country have the energy and consistency of Ginsu. At low tide, once you're past the dry reef section, the takeoff can throw out short, intense tubes before the wave starts to curve and bowl.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Table Top is a serious right-hand reef barrel on Puerto Rico's northwest corner, just north of Surfer's Beach and one of the first waves you reach coming around the point. It takes its name from the flat, exposed slab of reef that looks like a table, with the barrel spinning round right in front of the cliff over live coral. This is an expert-only wave: shallow, slabbing and sharp, with dangerous rocks on the inside and an exposed rock platform right at the takeoff.

Hazards include urchins, rips, rocks and pollution.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Tres Palmas is Puerto Rico's most famous big-wave break, a right-hander that peels off the last and furthest-out section of the long reef running down from Domes. A deepwater trench sits just outside, focusing long-period swell into big, meaty peaks that stand up fast and then open into long walls. Once you make the drop there's a large canvas ahead, roughly 75 yards of rumbling wall built for big, drawn-out turns rather than quick, flashy surfing.

guideText.text: Anse des Cayes on the North Coast is a fairly exposed reef break that has reasonably consistent surf. Winter and spring are the optimum times of year to visit. The best wind direction is from the south southwest. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the best swell direction is from the north northeast. Right and better left hand reef breaks.. Rarely crowded here. Beware of rocks, coral etc. Anse des Cayes

Anse des Cayes is a reef setup with two very different waves on offer. The left is mellow and can run a surprisingly long way when it lines up, while the right is hollow and finishes over a sketchy, super-shallow coral reef. Everything breaks over dead coral, so the two sides really do ask for different levels of comfort: the lefts suit intermediates, the rights are one for experts. When It Works Swell arrives from north through east, with northeast the direction that switches the reef on best. It works from 0.9 m / 3 ft to 2.4 m / 8 ft , and it is moderately consistent, so there are decent windows through the year rather than waves on demand. Wind and Tide Look for southwest offshore wind to clean it up. The reef can work through most of the tide, with a rising tide generally the better call. Local Tips Intermediates will get the most out of it by sticking to the left. Expect a fairly quiet lineup. Access There is free parking, with roadside spots close to the beach.

guideText.text: The Ledge on the North Coast is a fairly exposed reef break that has reasonably consistent surf. Winter and spring are the best times of year to visit. Works best in offshore winds from the south southwest. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the best swell direction is from the north northeast. A choice of left and right reefs. Rarely crowded here. Beware of rocks, coral etc. The Ledge

The Ledge is a shallow A-frame reef off Orient, the surfing hub of St Barths where the Reefer's Surf Club crew meet up before and after their sessions. The reef throws both lefts and rights over dead coral. When It Works It takes a decent north to northeast swell to switch on; without one the bay stays flat and fills with pleasure craft. Swell comes in from north through east, with north the best direction, and the reef works from 0.9 m / 3 ft to 2.4 m / 8 ft . Consistency is moderate, so expect it to come and go with the bigger pulses. Wind and Tide Look for a south offshore wind to clean it up. The reef can work through low, mid, and high tide, with a rising tide the better call. Local Tips This is an intermediate wave rather than a place to learn, and the local boys expect their pick of the sets. Expect a moderately busy lineup when it's on. Access There's free roadside parking.

guideText.text: Toiny on the South Coast is a fairly exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf The best wind direction is from the northwest. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the southeast. Right and better left hand reef breaks.. Rarely crowded here. Beware of rocks, coral etc. Toiny

Toiny sits on the southern side of the island and breaks over an uneven reef, firing off fast barrels in both directions. The right is short and gnarly, while the left is a long, glorious walling wave, and both run hollow and shallow. When Toiny is off, there are further fickle reef peaks to the west at each end of Grand Fond and Washing Machine. When It Works Facing south, Toiny relies on southern swells thrown up by summer and autumn hurricanes, or on big wrap-around swells from the northeast. It draws swell from northeast through east-southeast to south, with southeast (SE) the best match. The wave works from 0.9 m / 3 ft to 3 m / 10 ft . It tends to be somewhat inconsistent, so you'll want to catch it when the swell lines up. Wind and Tide Look for a northwest (NW) offshore wind. Because the reef is hollow and shallow, incoming water is best, so a rising tide is the better call even though it can break through low, mid, and high. Local Tips Toiny is a good option for intermediate surfers. The lineup is usually fairly quiet, though it can gather a crowd when it's working. Access There's free roadside parking nearby.
